summary: Defines SNMP management objects, using SMIv2, for monitoring and controlling devices that support HPR, High Performance Routing, in IBM SNA networks. It lets managers inspect those devices.

eli5.summary: It is a control panel layout for managers to check on a kind of old IBM network equipment.

questions: how to manage sna hpr with snmp
what is rtp in sna hpr
how to trigger an hpr path switch
subtitle: The SNMP object definitions for watching and nudging IBM SNA High Performance Routing nodes.

tldr.problem: Network devices that support HPR (High Performance Routing, an enhancement to IBM's APPN architecture) needed a standard way for management stations to inspect them over SNMP.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a MIB module, written in SMIv2, with four groups of objects: global node data, the ANR routing table, the users of the HPR transport, and the RTP connections with their path-switch history.
tldr.outcome: Managers can monitor HPR routing and connections and trigger a path switch, but the MIB does not configure HPR nodes, cover APPN-specific uses of HPR, or define traps.

today: RFC 2238 is a Proposed Standard published in November 1997. The unit metadata shows no RFC obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: What the HPR MIB Is For
sections.content:
RFC 2238 defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for monitoring and controlling network devices with HPR (High Performance Routing) capabilities. HPR is an enhancement to the Advanced Peer-to-Peer Network (APPN) architecture that provides fast data routing and improved session reliability. APPN is one protocol that can use the HPR transport mechanism.

The objects are written with SMIv2, the version 2 Structure of Management Information, which the RFC points to through RFC 1902, RFC 1903 and RFC 1904 (see RFC 1902). Management of APPN itself, and of its use of the HPR transport, belongs to the APPN MIB in RFC 2115.
sections.eli5: HPR is a fast way for computers in an old IBM network to pass messages along. This document is the list of things a network manager can look at to see how that is going.

sections.title: HPR Concepts the MIB Relies On
sections.content:
Automatic Network Routing (ANR) is a fast, low-level routing technique. Each node assigns a unique (within that node) ANR label to each out-bound link as it is activated. The ANR string, a group of labels, is encoded in a header in front of the message. At each hop the node strips off its own label and forwards the message on the link with that label. The last label is the Network Connection Endpoint (NCE), which identifies the component in the destination node that receives the message.

Rapid Transport Protocol (RTP) is an end-to-end, full duplex transport connection. It uses ANR, is connection-oriented, delivers data reliably and in order, and recovers from errors with selective retransmission. An RTP path can be switched without disrupting the sessions using it, either automatically when a link fails and another path exists, or on demand to try to restore the best path.

RTP does flow and congestion control with the Adaptive Rate-Based (ARB) algorithm, which runs only at the two ends of the connection. ARB adapts the sender's rate to feedback on the receiver's rate and is designed to prevent congestion rather than react to it.
sections.eli5: ANR is like a list of directions on an envelope, where each stop tears off its own line and passes the letter on. RTP is the pipe that carries the letters and can quietly switch to a different road if one is blocked.

sections.title: Structure of the MIB Module
sections.content:
The module hangs under snanauMIB (which is mib-2 34) as number 6. It contains four collections of objects:

  • hprGlobal: general HPR objects, such as the APPN control point name of the node and the level of support for operator-requested path switches.
  • hprAnrRouting: objects tied to the ANR routing table, plus controls for counting ANR packets.
  • hprTransportUser: the NCE table, which identifies network connection endpoints and their function types.
  • hprRtp: objects for the HPR Transport Tower, meaning the RTP connections.

HPR relies very little on the APPN MIB. The APPN object appnNodeCounterDisconTime is used to detect discontinuities in HPR counters, and hprNodeCpName has the same value as appnNodeCpName in the APPN MIB.
sections.eli5: The dials are sorted into four drawers: one for general facts, one for the direction-list routing table, one for who is using the network pipes, and one for the pipes themselves.

sections.title: Routing and Endpoint Tables
sections.content:
The hprAnrRoutingTable correlates an incoming ANR label, one assigned by this node, with the transmission group (TG) or local NCE the packet will be forwarded to. It is indexed by the label, an octet string of 1 to 8 octets. Each entry says whether the label identifies a local NCE or a TG, names the TG destination and number (these have no meaning for a local NCE), and counts the packets received with that label. A read-write object, hprAnrCounterState, lets a management station switch that packet counting on and off.

The hprNceTable identifies network connection endpoints and their function types. The HprNceTypes textual convention is a bit string with four bits: control point (bit 0), logical unit (bit 1), boundary function (bit 2) and route setup (bit 3). Any combination can apply to one NCE. The table also reports which function types an NCE is the default for, since some implementations provide default NCEs even though the architecture does not define them.
sections.eli5: One table says where each direction-list label sends a letter and counts how many came through. Another table lists the mailboxes in the building and what each one does.

sections.title: RTP Connections and Path Switches
sections.content:
The hprRtpTable has one entry for each RTP connection. An entry carries the local and remote NCE IDs and transport connection identifiers (TCIDs, 8 octets), the route selection control vector, the topic (used to indicate the Class of Service), timers, send rates, and statistics. The hprRtpState object reports the connection state from the local point of view: rtpListening, rtpCalling, rtpConnected, rtpPathSwitching, rtpDisconnecting or other.

A manager can trigger an operator-requested path switch by setting hprRtpPathSwitchTrigger to switchPathNow(2). The MIB cannot specify a new path. The read-only hprOperatorPathSwitchSupport object says how much the agent supports: not at all, a 'switch path now' command only, or also switching to a specified path through some other means such as a local operator interface.

The hprRtpStatusTable keeps history. An entry is created when a path switch completes, successfully or not, recording old and new route vectors, the start and end times, why the switch started and the result. How many entries to keep, and for how long, is an implementation choice. Counters in the RTP table can be turned on and off with hprRtpGlobeCtrState.
sections.eli5: Each pipe gets a row on the dashboard showing its health. You can press a 'find a new road now' button, and a logbook remembers every time the road was changed and whether it worked.

sections.title: What the MIB Leaves Out
sections.content: The module does not support configuration of HPR nodes, protocol-specific uses of HPR such as APPN, or traps. The APPN MIB contains a trap for Alert conditions that may affect HPR resources. The value of its affectedObject is determined by the implementation and may hold a VariablePointer into the HPR MIB.
sections.eli5: This dashboard only lets you look, plus press one button. You cannot use it to set the equipment up, and it does not ring an alarm by itself.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says MIBs are not themselves security risks if SNMP security is operating as intended. None of the read-only objects reports a password, user data or anything particularly sensitive, though some enterprises treat network configuration and usage information as corporate assets and may wish to restrict SNMP access to most objects.

One read-write object can affect network operations: hprRtpPathSwitchTrigger. A path switch does not itself disrupt the SNA sessions using the connection, but frequent switches on many RTP connections can hurt overall network performance. The RFC recommends restricting SNMP access to this object. The other read-write objects only control the gathering of management data, so controlling access to them is less critical.
sections.eli5: Looking at the dials is mostly harmless, but the 'switch roads' button should only be given to people you trust, because pressing it too often can slow everyone down.

viz.caption: OBJECT GROUPS OF THE HPR MIB MODULE

items.label: rtpListening
items.desc: Connection open; waiting for the other end to call in.

items.label: rtpCalling
items.desc: Attempting to call out; no data received from the other end yet.

items.label: rtpPathSwitching
items.desc: Path switch timer is running; looking for a new path.

items.label: rtpDisconnecting
items.desc: No sessions use the connection; it is being brought down.

items.label: other
items.desc: Not in any of the listed states.
